deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page continues the previous one (γ Draconis): reduction of meridian-circle transit observations, Göttingen 1818, to mean right ascension. The star here is labelled '6 Ursae' (identity not checked). Its 1818 place is α = 183°36'24" = 12h14m25.6s and δ = 88°42'8", so it is about 1°18' from the pole. The clock readings near 0h14m show these are LOWER culminations: clock time + 12h = α.

(A) TRANSIT TABLE ('Lauter einzelne Faden' = observed on single wires only).
- Columns: UZ = clock time of transit; clock correction ΔT; AR app = UZ + ΔT (+12h); reduction R (apparent − mean); AR med = AR app − R.
- Oct 27: 13'51.95" + 30.08 = 14'22.03"; 22.03 + 25.69 = 47.72.
- All of Oct 27 and Nov 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12 check exactly. Mean values: 47.72, 48.12, 47.81, 54.08, 49.43, 44.89, 40.04, 35.62.
- Nov 13, 15, 25 are rough: AR app ≈ 28, 30, 42 (clock correction ≈ 29–30 assumed). Means ≈ 44, 45, 49.
- The reductions R are linear interpolations in the 5-day table on the next page (−25.69 Oct 27, −23.25 Nov 1, −20.46 Nov 6, −17.35 Nov 11, −13.93 Nov 16, −10.19 Nov 21, −6.18 Nov 26). Examples: Nov 3 = −23.25 + 0.4·2.79 = −22.13; Nov 10 = −20.46 + 0.8·3.11 = −17.97; Nov 25 ≈ −10.19 + 0.8·4.01 = −6.98 ≈ −7.00.
- Final value 12h14m45.67s (my check): arithmetic mean of the first ten values, Oct 27–Nov 15, using the rounded 44 and 45 and omitting Nov 25: 456.71/10 = 45.671.

(B) STAR CONSTANTS ('Constanten für diesen Stern'). Logarithms with n = negative.
- log cos α = 9.99914n, log sin α = 8.79869n.
- log cos δ = 8.35503, log sin δ = 9.99989, log tan δ = 1.64485.
- Hence log sec δ = 1.64497 and log sin α tan δ = 0.44354n (written in column 3).
- log cos α sin δ = 9.99903n and log sin α sin δ = 8.79858n.
- In column 3 the factor log cos α tan δ is 1.64399n. The transcription's 1.64499 is a misreading; the sum 0.95124 + 1.64399 = 2.59523 confirms it.

Method. Each periodic term c1·cos x + c2·sin x is rewritten as A·sin(x + B), with A sin B = c1 and A cos B = c2. B is found from tan B = c1/c2. A is found as c1/sin B or c2/cos B; sec B is taken from log sin/cos B, i.e. by Gaussian logarithms. Here x = ⊙ for aberration, Ω for lunar nutation, and 2⊙ for solar nutation. This is Gauss's own A·sin(⊙+B) scheme from his aberration/nutation tables.

Col 1, aberration in RA. Formula: Δα = −k secδ (cosε cosα cos⊙ + sinα sin⊙).
- log(−k cosε) = 1.27660n and log(−k) = 1.31408n, i.e. k ≈ 20.61".
- The difference 9.96252 = log cos ε, giving ε ≈ 23°28'.
- c1 = 1.27660n + 1.64411n (cosα secδ) = 2.92071.
- c2 = 1.31408n + 0.44366n (sinα secδ) = 1.75774.
- tan B → B = 86°4'19"; log sin B = 9.99898; A = 2.92173 (≈835").
- Minus log 15 = 1.17609 gives 1.74564 in seconds of time; this value is used on the next page.

Col 2, aberration in declination. Formula: Δδ = −k[cos⊙(sinε cosδ − cosε sinα sinδ) + sin⊙ cosα sinδ].
- −k sinε: 0.91416n.
- c1 = 0.91416n·8.35503 → 9.26919n, plus 1.27660·8.79858n → 0.07518n. The Gaussian addition log 0.06308 gives the sum 0.13826n.
- c2 = 1.31408n·9.99903n = 1.31311.
- B = 356°10'30"; cos B 9.99903; A = 1.31408 (= k, as expected near the pole).

Col 3, lunar nutation in RA. Formula: Δα = −P(cosε + sinε sinα tanδ) sinΩ − Q cosα tanδ cosΩ.
- log P = 1.22302 (P ≈ 16.71"), written '−1.22302' at the top; log Q = 0.95124 (Q ≈ 8.94").
- Hence P sinε → 0.82308 and P cosε → 1.18552.
- c1 (cosΩ) = 0.95124n·1.64399n = 2.59523.
- c2 (sinΩ) = 0.82308n·0.44354n, written 0.86662, plus 1.18552n. Gaussian subtraction log 0.28386 gives 0.90166n.
- B = 91°9'36" (2nd quadrant); log sin B 9.99991; A = 2.59534.

Col 4, lunar nutation in declination. Formula: Δδ = −P sinε cosα sinΩ + Q sinα cosΩ.
- c1 = 0.95124·8.79869n, written 9.74973n.
- c2 = 0.82308n·9.99914n = 0.82222.
- B = 355°9'46"; cos B 9.99845; A = 0.82377 (≈6.66").

Col 5, solar nutation in RA (argument 2⊙, P' = 1", Q' ≈ 0.434").
- c1 = 1.28148 (= log Q' + 1.64399).
- c2 = 9.67864n = 0.90166n − 1.22302, i.e. the column-3 factor rescaled from P to P' = 1.
- B = 91°25'46"; log sin B 9.99986; A = 1.28162.

Col 6, solar nutation in declination.
- c1 = 8.43598n (Q' sinα).
- c2 = 9.59920 (= sinε·cosα with P' = 1).
- B = 356°4'17"; cos B 9.99898; A = 9.60022.

The next page uses exactly these values: 1.74564 / 86.4, 1.31408 / 356.10, 91.10 / 355.10 with Ω, and 91.26 / 356.4 with 2⊙. The source of the top-right value '−1.31375' (log ≈ 20.59) is unclear.

(C) TIME OF TRANSIT (bottom right; tentative).
- 14h4m52s ≈ the Sun's RA on Oct 27 (sidereal time at apparent noon).
- 0h14m26s = sidereal time of the star's lower transit.
- Their difference 24h14m26 − 14h4m52 = 10h9m34s = 10.1595 h (so the written '10.9.57' is probably 10.9.34).
- Converted to mean time this is ≈ 10h7m54s = 0.422 d. This gives the epoch 300.422 (day of year 1818: Oct 27 = day 300) on the next page.
- The remaining entries (4.23, 16.49.43, 7.24.72, 7.412, 30) are not securely interpretable.
errors: Column 3: 0.82308 + 0.44354 = 1.26662, but Gauss wrote 0.86662 (characteristic off by 0.4). The true sinΩ coefficient in the lunar RA nutation is +18.48 − 15.33 = +3.14 (log 0.4976), not −7.98 (0.90166n). So B should be ≈89°32.5', not 91°9'36". A is essentially unchanged (≈393.7"). The error of up to ≈11" of arc (≈0.7 s of time) propagates to the RA reductions on the next page, which uses 91.10.
Column 5 inherits the same slip: c2 = 9.67864n should be ≈ +9.2746 (+0.188). B should then be ≈89°26' instead of 91°25'46" (error up to ≈0.65" of arc).
Column 4: 0.95124 + 8.79869 = 9.74993, written 9.74973. B changes only from 355°9'37" to 355°9'46"; negligible.
Column 1: arctan(10^1.16297) gives B ≈ 86°4'9", Gauss has 86°4'19" (≈10" difference; negligible).
Minor last-digit discrepancies: column 3 A = 2.59523 − 9.99991 = 2.59532 (written 2.59534); column 6 Q' sinα ≈ 8.43618 vs 8.43598.
The aberration constant implied by log 1.31408 is ≈20.61", larger than the contemporary 20.25–20.45". Not necessarily an error, but unusual; its basis is unclear.

results.what: Reduction of lower-culmination transits of a near-polar star to mean RA. Clock correction is applied, reductions are linearly interpolated, and the observations are averaged to 12h14m45.67s.

Star constants for aberration (argument ⊙), lunar nutation (Ω) and solar nutation (2⊙) in RA and declination, each cast as A·sin(arg + B) and evaluated with logarithms and Gaussian addition/subtraction logarithms.
results.modern_name: Star constants / independent day numbers (precursor of Besselian A,B,C,D / a,b,c,d)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's own aberration/nutation tables (Monatliche Correspondenz, c.1806–08); Bessel, Tabulae Regiomontanae (1830)

results.what: Conversion of sidereal transit time to mean time of observation (epoch 300.422 days) using the Sun's RA.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine observatory reduction work in Gauss's own known tabular formalism. The only notable items are an arithmetic slip (0.86662 for 1.26662) that propagates into his nutation constants for this star, and an apparently high aberration constant (≈20.61"). These are of minor archival interest only.

transcription_corrections: Column 3, line 2: '1.64499n' should read 1.64399n (log cosα tanδ); confirmed by 0.95124 + 1.64399 = 2.59523.
Bottom right: '10.9.57' is probably 10.9.34, since 10.1595 h = 10h9m34s = 24h14m26 − 14h4m52.
In the first data row the '12' of 12h14'22"03 is written over another figure; the AR app column is 12h + clock time + correction.
The second numeric column (30.08, 30.54, …) is the clock correction; the column after AR app is the reduction (app − mean).
The rough entries for Nov 13/15/25 (28, 30, 42 and 44, 45, 49) are approximate values, not truncations.
